Administrative Constitutionalism. It is common for Congress to leave 
to an administrative agency the job of filhng in some (or all) of the procedural 
details under a statute that calls for implementation via adjudication. (As 
under the AUMF, discussed immediately above.) To fulfill this responsibility, 
the agency must apply Mathews to determine what constitutional due process 
requires. In many instances, the agency’s determination will not be reviewed 
(or will be reviewed very deferentially) by an Article III court. The practical 
consequence is that agencies themselves are now the primary frontline 
expositors and appliers of the Mathews test. Administrative constitutionalism 
has already come to the Due Process Clause.” Adnan Vermeule, Deference and 
Due Process, 129 Ha r v . L. Re v . 1890, 1891 (2016).
2. THE INTERESTS PROTECTED BY DUE 
PROCESS HEARING RIGHTS
a. The Right/Privilege Distinction and Its “Demise”
The Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments provide identically that due 
process of law is a prerequisite to any denial of “life, liberty, or property.” 
This is a conspicuously ambiguous text. One could read “life, liberty, or 
property” as an elegant way of encompassing everything that people hold 
important. So read, the Due Process Clause would be applicable to all 
government decisions that affect individuals in important ways—or, given 
Londoner v. Denver, supra, at least all such decisions that are 
adjudicatory’ in nature. Alternatively, one could read “life, liberty, or 
property as historically fixed categories with specific common law 
referents.
Until the 1950s, the latter, narrow reading prevailed—or, perhaps 
niore accurately, was presumed. The relevant cases, often without serious 
discussion, invoked a distinction between common law property rights, 
protected by due process, and mere privileges or governmp.nt largesse, 
whose disposition was subject only to those procedures that the 
government chose to provide. Although uttered in a First, rather than a 
Fifth Amendment context. Justice Holmes’ remark that a person may have 
the right to talk politics but not to be a police officer is the pithiest 
expression of the right/privilege distinction. McAuliffe v. Mayor of New 
Bedford, 155 Mass. 216, 220, 29 N.E. 517 (1892).
